doc.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998

title: Nicholas Payton and the Doc Cheatham duet album
summary: Young black musicians lack the foundation; Payton is the exception, and led to the Grammy-winning Stardust duets with Cheatham.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: From what I see, and please correct me if I’m wrong, it seems like the mainstream tradition that’s being carried on in jazz today is mostly the white musicians — Ken Peplowski and Randy —

Oh yes it’s certainly true. But there’s a reason for it, which is a very unfortunate one. And that is that the younger white musicians don’t know the foundation of what they consider their music. They simply don’t go into it and—
I’m sorry, the younger white musicians?

The younger black musicians, did I say white? The younger black musicians don’t know the origins of jazz and they don’t know say the New Orleans tradition except for those who are down in New Orleans. A great example of the positive side of a young black musician knowing the foundation of the music is Nicholas Payton. I consider Nicholas to be the outstanding young jazz musician in the world today, by a considerable margin, and one reason is that he not only knows the music from the beginning on, but he can play it. I mean he plays Louis Armstrong and the early New Orleans pioneers and the swing people to perfection and he is also the closest thing I’ve heard to say Clifford Brown. He knows the whole bop era and he plays it. When he plays in person, whatever happens, you can hear the whole history of jazz because he basically plays the modern aspect of jazz but then he dips into the earlier music as well. And the most striking example of that was the few performances he made in New York in which he had guests on different nights during the week that he played say at the Iridium. He would have Clark Terry for one or two nights, and then he would have Doc Cheatham for one or two nights, and so his sets were like a kind of history of jazz in which he would start out with his modern group and then gradually get back into the past of jazz, not all the way back of course. And out of that came a wonderful recording which won a Grammy award thank © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
goodness, and that was the duet album with Doc Cheatham and the performance of “Stardust.” I can’t even talk about it.
I know. It’s great to listen.

I’m so happy that it happened, and it happened under odd circumstances. It almost didn’t happen but there was a lady named Andrea — oh God all of a sudden I’m drawing a blank on her last name, it’s a very nice French name, she’s from New Orleans — and she was the one who thought of the idea and pushed it though. And she represented Doc Cheatham in his later years, actually managing him out of New Orleans. Anyway you can get the story of that basically from the CD, which is one of the most delightful records in recent years.
